<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Boyuan An,
Zhexiong Wang<sup id="id1" class="ltx_sup">*</sup>,
Yipeng Wang<sup id="id2" class="ltx_sup">*</sup>,
Jiaqi Li,
Sihang Li<sup id="id3" class="ltx_sup">†</sup>,
Jing Zhang<sup id="id4" class="ltx_sup">†</sup>,
Chen Feng<sup id="id5" class="ltx_sup">†</sup>
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>
New York University

</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Humans can rearrange objects in cluttered environments using egocentric perception, navigating occlusions without global coordinates.
Inspired by this capability, we study long-horizon multi-object non-prehensile rearrangement for mobile robots using a single egocentric camera.
We introduce EgoPush, a policy learning framework that enables egocentric, perception-driven rearrangement without relying on explicit global state estimation that often fails in dynamic scenes.
EgoPush designs an object-centric latent space to encode relative spatial relations among objects, rather than absolute poses.
This design enables a privileged reinforcement-learning (RL) teacher to jointly learn latent states and mobile actions from sparse keypoints, which is then distilled into a purely visual student policy.
To reduce the supervision gap between the omniscient teacher and the partially observed student, we restrict the teacher’s observations to visually accessible cues.
This induces active perception behaviors that are recoverable from the student’s viewpoint.
To address long-horizon credit assignment, we decompose rearrangement into stage-level subproblems using temporally decayed, stage-local completion rewards.
Extensive simulation experiments demonstrate that EgoPush significantly outperforms end-to-end RL baselines in success rate, with ablation studies validating each design choice. 
We further demonstrate zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on a mobile platform in the real world.
Code and videos can be found at <a href="https://ai4ce.github.io/EgoPush/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://ai4ce.github.io/EgoPush/</a>.</p>
  
</div><span id="footnotex1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnotetext"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">footnotetext: </span>Equal Contribution</span></span></span><span id="footnotex2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnotetext"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">footnotetext: </span>Corresponding Authors, {<a href="mailto:sl10496@nyu.edu" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">sl10496</a>, <a href="mailto:jz6676@nyu.edu" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">z.jing</a>, <a href="mailto:cfeng@nyu.edu" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">cfeng</a>}@nyu.edu</span></span></span>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">I </span><span id="S1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Introduction</span></h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Humans routinely perform long-horizon rearrangement in cluttered spaces without consulting precise <em id="S1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">global</em> coordinates. Instead, they maintain an egocentric sense of <em id="S1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">relative</em> spatial relations and continuously coordinate motion to keep task-relevant cues in view under intermittent occlusions. For instance, one can reposition several chairs into a symmetric arrangement around a table by repeatedly stepping around to re-check alignment when chairs occlude one another.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Replicating this capability on robotic platforms is highly impactful, yet far from trivial. We introduce a controlled testbed: multi-object non-prehensile rearrangement from purely egocentric visual observations.
The task challenges a mobile robot to operate over long horizons: it must navigate and physically nudge multiple robot-scale objects precisely into predefined arrangements relative to an anchor object (<em id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">e.g</em>., cross-shaped or linear patterns in Fig. <span class="ltx_ref ltx_missing_label ltx_ref_self"></span>).
Our environment is intentionally texture sparse, containing no external landmarks or visual references beyond the objects themselves.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">This setting poses several coupled challenges for egocentric mobile rearrangement:
texture-sparse observations provide no reliable landmarks.
During contact-rich interaction, objects are continuously displaced and frequently occlude one another, further challenging egocentric perception.
Consequently, the agent cannot assume reliable global localization or external references, and must instead coordinate actions using only perceived relative relations between the robot and objects.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Existing methodologies struggle in this setting, as most non-prehensile manipulation frameworks rely on global state or external tracking <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>, <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>, <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>, <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>, <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite>.
Model-based approaches are particularly brittle:
texture-sparse scenes challenge SLAM or visual odometry <em id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">to maintain consistent localization during object motion</em>; and during contact-rich interactions, the continual object motion violates the static-world assumptions commonly used in geometric mapping.
Without stable global localization, planners lack a consistent reference frame and can degrade substantially.
In contrast, standard end-to-end reinforcement learning (RL) directly <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>, <a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>, <a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>, <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite> from egocentric pixels avoids explicit mapping, but often suffers from poor sample efficiency and brittleness under partial observability caused by occlusions. When key cues repeatedly disappear from view, policies can fail to maintain coherent strategies for egocentric mobile manipulation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">A natural direction to improve sample efficiency is cross-modal distillation:
training a privileged teacher with low-dimensional environment states via online RL, then distilling its behavior into an egocentric visual student <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">47</a>, <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>, <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>, <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>, <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>, <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>, <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>, <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>]</cite>.
However, in our setting, this direction faces two core challenges: (1) the observability gap in distillation, and (2) long-horizon credit assignment.
First, conventional pipeline typically optimizes an omniscient teacher under global ground-truth observations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">47</a>, <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>, <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>]</cite> and uses its behavior as supervision.
In our setting, this can be counterproductive:
because perception and action are tightly coupled, an all-seeing teacher may execute trajectories that are irrecoverable from the student’s egocentric view—
for example, moving backward toward a target object behind the robot without turning to bring the object into view, yielding action labels that are inexplicable given the student’s limited field of view.
The student then receives inconsistent supervision, becomes brittle, and fails to ground its policy in visually accessible evidence.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Beyond the observability gap, the long-horizon nature of multi-object tasks presents another bottleneck: temporal credit assignment.
Without explicit temporal decomposition, a vanilla RL formulation treats these tasks as monolithic sequences, where sparse rewards fail to distinguish efficient maneuvers from aimless exploration.
As the episode unfolds, the learning signal becomes increasingly delayed and attenuated, making it difficult for the agent to acquire the precise, tightly coordinated behaviors required for task completion.
Consequently, without an explicit mechanism to provide dense and comparable progress signals throughout the entire sequence, optimization can fail or converge to suboptimal strategies.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">To address these challenges, we present EgoPush, a policy learning framework for long-horizon multi-object rearrangement from egocentric vision.
It learns object-centric representations that capture task-relevant <em id="S1.p7.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">relative</em> spatial relations among the objects, enabling rearrangement without explicit global state estimation.
To make teacher–student distillation viable under partial observability, we introduce Constrained Teacher RL, which limits the privileged teacher to egocentric, visibility-limited observations so that its behavior remains reproducible from the student’s viewpoint and induces learnable active perception.
Finally, it improves temporal credit assignment for long-horizon tasks via stage-wise training with temporally decayed, stage-local completion rewards.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate EgoPush in extensive simulation benchmarks and further demonstrate successful zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on a Turtlebot mobile platform.
Across baseline comparisons and ablation studies, EgoPush consistently improves both success rate and sample efficiency over alternative designs.
We achieve robust transfer by explicitly modeling depth noise in simulation and mitigating sensor noise on real hardware.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p9.1" class="ltx_p">To summarize our contributions of EgoPush, a policy training framework using cross-modal teacher–student distillation:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">It enables multi-object rearrangement from purely egocentric vision without relying on explicit maps or global positioning, by learning object-centric latent representations that encode relative spatial relations;</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">It induces learnable active perception behaviors that jointly handle mobility, perception, and object interaction, by constraining the privileged teacher to egocentric, visibility-limited observations;</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">It facilitates long-horizon learning with improved temporal credit assignment through a stage-aligned reward that decomposes complex tasks into manageable subproblems;</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Its key designs are validated through extensive baseline comparisons and ablation studies, with successful zero-shot sim-to-real transfers.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">II </span><span id="S2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Related Works</span></h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S2.SS1.6" class="ltx_text">II-A</span> </span><span id="S2.SS1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Non-prehensile Mobile Manipulation</span></h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Non-prehensile manipulation is a practical cornerstone for mobile robots in clutter, as it allows interaction with objects that are infeasible to grasp due to size, weight, density, or accessibility constraints.
For example, it can facilitate <em id="S2.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">navigation</em> by pushing aside movable obstacles to unlock a traversable passage or reduce local congestion <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>, <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>, <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite>,
accomplish <em id="S2.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">rearrangement</em> by relocating objects to satisfy task goals <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite>,
and perform <em id="S2.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">reconfiguration</em> by driving an object into a more favorable pose for subsequent operations (<em id="S2.SS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">e.g</em>., improving stability or exposing a useful face) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>, <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Classic solutions typically frame non-prehensile rearrangement as planning/optimization under contact dynamics.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Song et al. [35]</a></cite> formulates planar sorting with Monte Carlo Tree Search to reason over contact-induced transitions,
while <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ren et al. [30]</a></cite> structures the problem from an object-centric viewpoint to facilitate decision-making in cluttered scenes.
Hybrid pipelines further combine task-and-motion planning with learned non-prehensile skills to handle complex interaction modes <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>]</cite>;
other works <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>, <a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite> incorporates additional sensing modalities (<em id="S2.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">e.g</em>., force or tactile feedback) to support pushing with a mobile base.
Despite their strong long-horizon performance, these systems commonly assume access to accurate robot/object states or an explicit state estimator—requirements that can be brittle or infeasible when only egocentric sensing is available.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Vision-based learning improves generalization across object properties <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>, <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>]</cite>, yet many non-prehensile rearrangement pipelines still rely on global state.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al. [41]</a></cite> relies on top-down reconstructions together with a known global map to build spatial action representations.
Multi-agent pushing is likewise commonly studied under global-information assumptions to enable coordination <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>, <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>]</cite>. Other systems explicitly introduce privileged viewpoints, such as aerial bird’s-eye-view guidance for ground robots <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite>.
Even in purely “visual” rearrangement, some setups effectively provide global coverage by keeping all objects within the camera frustum <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite>.
Consequently, a key open challenge remains: achieving long-horizon non-prehensile rearrangement under <em id="S2.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">genuinely</em> partial observability, where egocentric views are narrow, occlusions are frequent, and global state is not accessible.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S2.SS2.6" class="ltx_text">II-B</span> </span><span id="S2.SS2.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Visual Policy Learning of Mobile Robots</span></h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Learning robot control from visual observations is a long-standing direction for reducing reliance on explicit state estimation.
A straightforward paradigm is end-to-end RL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>, <a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>, <a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>, <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite>, which maps high-dimensional images (often fused with proprioception) directly to actions.
Although RL has made notable progress in state-based learning of mobile robots <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>, <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>, <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>, <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">44</a>]</cite>, pixel-based RL learning remains sample-inefficient and sensitive to reward sparsity and partial observability,
motivating a wide range of techniques to improve stability and data efficiency (<em id="S2.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">e.g</em>., stronger visual encoders <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">46</a>, <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>, <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>,
asymmetric actor-critic <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite>, parallel differentiable simulation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>]</cite>, using low-dimensional visual features <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>]</cite>, etc.).
However, contact-rich mobile manipulation introduces a more severe form of partial observability.  
Visual signals are inherently sparse during execution: pushing actions not only result in frequent self-occlusions but also often displace objects outside the camera frustum.
This lack of persistent visual grounding causes purely reactive pixel-based policies to fail, as they overfit to transient cues and lack the robustness to recover from prolonged periods of visual vacancy.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A complementary and often more data-efficient pipeline is privileged RL teacher–visual student distillation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">47</a>, <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>, <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>, <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>, <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>, <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>, <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>, <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>]</cite>.
The common recipe is to train a teacher policy with access to privileged signals available in simulation—
<em id="S2.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">e.g</em>.<span id="S2.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text"></span>, global ground-truth state <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">47</a>, <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>, <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>]</cite>,
noiseless geometry <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>, <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>, <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite>,
or full-scene information unaffected by occlusion <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>, <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>]</cite>—
and then transfer its behavior to a visual student via imitation learning (behavior cloning) or interactive variants (DAgger <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>]</cite>).
This strategy has been effective across various visuomotor control problems because the teacher provides stable supervision that mitigates high-variance credit assignment from raw images.
Nevertheless, such benefits typically rely on an implicit assumption:
the teacher’s demonstrations are <em id="S2.SS2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">recoverable</em> from the student’s observation stream.
For egocentric mobile manipulation tasks where perception and action are tightly coupled,
an omniscient teacher optimized in the full state space can exploit off-screen or globally available information to execute trajectories that provide little visual evidence for a camera-based student.
As a result, the student may face an ill-posed imitation problem, where multiple teacher actions are consistent with the same partial observation, leading to ambiguous supervision and brittle downstream policies.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">III </span><span id="S3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Method</span></h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we first introduce an object-centric latent representation that abstracts the scene into task-relevant roles (Sec. <a href="#S3.SS1" title="III-A Object-Centric Latent Representation ‣ III Method ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">III-A</span></a>), serving as a shared interface for both teacher and student policies.
Then we introduce EgoPush, a two-phase distillation framework for long-horizon, multi-object non-prehensile rearrangement under egocentric observations.
Phase 1 performs online reinforcement learning under constrained privileged observations to train the teacher (Sec. <a href="#S3.SS2" title="III-B Phase 1 (Teacher): Online Reinforcement Learning ‣ III Method ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">III-B</span></a>).
Phase 2 distills the teacher’s behavior and intermediate representations into an egocentric visual student via imitation learning (Sec. <a href="#S3.SS3" title="III-C Phase 2 (Student): Supervised Learning ‣ III Method ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">III-C</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S3.SS1.6" class="ltx_text">III-A</span> </span><span id="S3.SS1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Object-Centric Latent Representation</span></h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For this rearrangement task, not all objects are equally important for decision-making. Within a pushing episode, the policy primarily needs to attend to the currently manipulated object (<span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">active object</span>) and the object that indicates the target (<span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">anchor</span>), while treating all remaining objects as obstacles (<span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">obstacle</span>). Therefore, we partition scene objects into three semantic categories and encode them with a shared-weight state estimator. This produces group-wise latent embeddings, which we concatenate to form a <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">object-centric latent representation</span>. Weight sharing aligns the geometric features of different groups in a common embedding space, enabling the policy to reason over <em id="S3.SS1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">relative spatial relations between group latents</em> rather than modeling each object in isolation.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S3.SS2.6" class="ltx_text">III-B</span> </span><span id="S3.SS2.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Phase 1 (Teacher): Online Reinforcement Learning</span></h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Action Space</span>.
The robot is a differential-drive base, and the policy outputs a 2D continuous action <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{t}=[v_{t},\ \omega_{t}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.667em">,</mo><msub><mi>ω</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{t}=[v_{t},\ \omega_{t}]</annotation></semantics></math>. <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is the base linear velocity and <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\omega_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ω</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\omega_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is the angular velocity, which are then converted into left/right wheel velocities via differential-drive kinematics and executed by PD controller.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Privileged Information: Sparse Keypoints</span>.
The teacher observes sparse keypoints <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>, <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>]</cite> for the active object, anchor, and obstacles that capture object geometry and their relative poses, which substantially reduces observation dimensionality and improves sample efficiency, while remaining sufficient for contact-rich pushing decisions. Since the objective is to push the active object near the anchor and align its pose, we additionally provide a target reference keypoint set <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{t}^{\text{ref}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>P</mi><mi>t</mi><mtext>ref</mtext></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{t}^{\text{ref}}</annotation></semantics></math> sampled from the keypoints of the predefined target configuration; for each task category, the relative pose between the anchor and the reference target is invariant across episodes, so <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{t}^{\text{ref}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>P</mi><mi>t</mi><mtext>ref</mtext></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{t}^{\text{ref}}</annotation></semantics></math> serves as a consistent spatial guide for pose alignment.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Constrained Observations</span>.
To ensure the teacher trajectories rely only on task-relevant information that is recoverable from the egocentric viewpoint and thus reproducible by the student, we impose two constraints. (1) <span id="S3.SS2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Virtual egocentric FOV masking</span>: we define a robot-pose-based viewing frustum and uniformly mask points outside the frustum or beyond a maximum range. This approximates the camera-visible field of view. (2) <span id="S3.SS2.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Center-gated visibility for <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{t}^{\text{ref}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>P</mi><mi>t</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">ref</mtext></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{t}^{\text{ref}}</annotation></semantics></math></span>: <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{t}^{\text{ref}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>P</mi><mi>t</mi><mtext>ref</mtext></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{t}^{\text{ref}}</annotation></semantics></math> is visible only when the anchor lies within the virtual FOV and lies inside a central gated region in the view, i.e., its normalized image-plane coordinates within <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\pm u_{\text{gate}},\pm v_{\text{gate}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo>±</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mtext>gate</mtext></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>±</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mtext>gate</mtext></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\pm u_{\text{gate}},\pm v_{\text{gate}})</annotation></semantics></math>. Otherwise, <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{t}^{\text{ref}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>P</mi><mi>t</mi><mtext>ref</mtext></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{t}^{\text{ref}}</annotation></semantics></math> is masked to prevent the policy from exploiting the reference while ignoring the anchor. Under these constraints, the teacher observes grouped sparse keypoints <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{P_{t}^{\text{act}},P_{t}^{\text{anc}},P_{t}^{\text{obs}},P_{t}^{\text{ref}}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>P</mi><mi>t</mi><mtext>act</mtext></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>P</mi><mi>t</mi><mtext>anc</mtext></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>P</mi><mi>t</mi><mtext>obs</mtext></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>P</mi><mi>t</mi><mtext>ref</mtext></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{P_{t}^{\text{act}},P_{t}^{\text{anc}},P_{t}^{\text{obs}},P_{t}^{\text{ref}}\}</annotation></semantics></math> and the previous action <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{t-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{t-1}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18071v1/main_2.png" id="S3.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/208;" width="476" height="208" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Fig. 1</span>: </span><span id="S3.F1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">EgoPush Overview<span id="S3.F1.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">. EgoPush is a two-phase learning framework for long-horizon, multi-object non-prehensile rearrangement under egocentric observations: in Phase 1, a privileged teacher policy is trained from sparse keypoints while enforcing egocentric, visibility-limited sensing so its behaviors remain visually recoverable; in Phase 2, an egocentric student uses RGB only for instance grouping and receives group-wise depth inputs, and is distilled online from the teacher via latent and action regression, enabling zero-shot sim-to-real deployment on a TurtleBot with a RealSense camera. </span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p4.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p4.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Rewards.</span>
Our rewards include: (1) <span id="S3.SS2.p4.2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Stage-aligned completion reward</span>: In long-horizon sequential rearrangement, the agent repeatedly solves similar subproblems (reach the active object<math id="S3.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> place it near anchor) under delayed and sparse feedback.
Consequently, a binary completion reward provides limited guidance and tends to blur efficient and inefficient solutions.
We address this by (i) imposing a per-stage step budget <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T_{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T_{s}</annotation></semantics></math>, and (ii) weighting completion rewards by the fraction of remaining budget, yielding stage-aligned supervision.
Concretely, the <em id="S3.SS2.p4.2.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">reach</em> completion reward is</p>
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="r_{\text{reach},t}=\eta_{t}\cdot\mathbb{I}\!\left[\|\mathbf{p}_{\text{rbt},t}-\mathbf{p}_{\text{act},t}\|_{2}&lt;\varepsilon_{\text{reach}}\right]," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mtext>reach</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>η</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mpadded style="width:0.219em;" width="0.219em"><mi>𝕀</mi></mpadded><mrow><mo>[</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∥</mo><msub><mi>𝐩</mi><mrow><mtext>rbt</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝐩</mi><mrow><mtext>act</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.0835em">∥</mo><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0.0835em">&lt;</mo><msub><mi>ε</mi><mtext>reach</mtext></msub><mo>]</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{\text{reach},t}=\eta_{t}\cdot\mathbb{I}\!\left[\|\mathbf{p}_{\text{rbt},t}-\mathbf{p}_{\text{act},t}\|_{2}&lt;\varepsilon_{\text{reach}}\right],</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p4.3" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{p}_{\text{rbt},t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐩</mi><mrow><mtext>rbt</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{p}_{\text{rbt},t}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{p}_{\text{act},t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐩</mi><mrow><mtext>act</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{p}_{\text{act},t}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the 2D positions of the robot and the active object at time <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\varepsilon_{\text{reach}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ε</mi><mtext>reach</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varepsilon_{\text{reach}}</annotation></semantics></math> is the reaching threshold, and <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{I}[\cdot]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝕀</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{I}[\cdot]</annotation></semantics></math> is the indicator function that equals <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math> if the condition holds and <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math> otherwise.
We set</p>
<table id="S3.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\eta_{t}=\frac{T_{s}-\tau_{t}}{T_{s}+\epsilon_{0}}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>η</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>ϵ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\eta_{t}=\frac{T_{s}-\tau_{t}}{T_{s}+\epsilon_{0}},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p4.4" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is the stage-local elapsed steps (reset at each stage boundary), and <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ϵ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> is a small constant for numerical stability.
This time-weighted completion reward shortens effective credit assignment within a stage and provides a consistent incentive for timely completion,
which empirically stabilizes optimization and improves success in our long-horizon setting.
Similarly, the <em id="S3.SS2.p4.4.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">place</em> completion reward is</p>
<table id="S3.E3" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="S3.E3X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E3X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle r_{\text{place},t}=" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mtext>place</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mphantom></mphantom></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle r_{\text{place},t}=</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E3X.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\eta_{t}\,\mathbb{I}\!\Bigg[\begin{array}[]{cr}\|\mathbf{p}_{\text{act},t}-\mathbf{p}_{\text{ref},t}\|_{2}&lt;\varepsilon_{\text{align}}&amp;\text{and}\\
|\Delta\psi_{t}|&lt;\varepsilon_{\Phi}&amp;\text{and}\\
\|\mathbf{v}_{\text{act},t}\|_{2}&lt;\varepsilon_{v}&amp;\end{array}\Bigg]," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>η</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mpadded style="width:0.219em;" width="0.219em"><mi>𝕀</mi></mpadded><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="2.600em" minsize="2.600em">[</mo><mtable columnspacing="5pt" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐩</mi><mrow><mtext>act</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝐩</mi><mrow><mtext>ref</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><msub><mi>ε</mi><mtext>align</mtext></msub></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_right" columnalign="right"><mtext>and</mtext></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ψ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><msub><mi>ε</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi></msub></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_right" columnalign="right"><mtext>and</mtext></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mi>𝐯</mi><mrow><mtext>act</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><msub><mi>ε</mi><mi>v</mi></msub></mrow></mtd><mtd></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo maxsize="2.600em" minsize="2.600em">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\eta_{t}\,\mathbb{I}\!\Bigg[\begin{array}[]{cr}\|\mathbf{p}_{\text{act},t}-\mathbf{p}_{\text{ref},t}\|_{2}&lt;\varepsilon_{\text{align}}&amp;\text{and}\\
|\Delta\psi_{t}|&lt;\varepsilon_{\Phi}&amp;\text{and}\\
\|\mathbf{v}_{\text{act},t}\|_{2}&lt;\varepsilon_{v}&amp;\end{array}\Bigg],</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p4.5" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{p}_{\text{ref},t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐩</mi><mrow><mtext>ref</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{p}_{\text{ref},t}</annotation></semantics></math> is the 2D reference target position (defined by the virtual <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{t}^{\text{ref}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>P</mi><mi>t</mi><mtext>ref</mtext></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{t}^{\text{ref}}</annotation></semantics></math>), <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\varepsilon_{\text{align}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ε</mi><mtext>align</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varepsilon_{\text{align}}</annotation></semantics></math> is the position-alignment threshold, <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta\psi_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ψ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta\psi_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is the yaw error between the active object and its target orientation, and <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{v}_{\text{act},t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐯</mi><mrow><mtext>act</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{v}_{\text{act},t}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the planar velocity vector of the active object.
The thresholds <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\varepsilon_{\Phi},\varepsilon_{v})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>ε</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>ε</mi><mi>v</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\varepsilon_{\Phi},\varepsilon_{v})</annotation></semantics></math> ensure that the reward is only granted when the object is both precisely oriented and physically stable at the target location.
(2) <span id="S3.SS2.p4.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Progress shaping (Phase-Gated Distance Decrease)</span>:</p>
<table id="S3.E4" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="S3.E4X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E4X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle r_{\text{dist},t}=" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mtext>dist</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mphantom></mphantom></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle r_{\text{dist},t}=</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E4X.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle w_{\text{rbt}}\left(d_{\text{rbt},t-1}-d_{\text{rbt},t}\right)\,\mathbb{I}[g_{t}=0]\;" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>w</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>rbt</mtext></msub><mo>(</mo><mi>d</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mtext>rbt</mtext><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>d</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mtext>rbt</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo rspace="0.170em">)</mo><mi>𝕀</mi><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>g</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle w_{\text{rbt}}\left(d_{\text{rbt},t-1}-d_{\text{rbt},t}\right)\,\mathbb{I}[g_{t}=0]\;</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="2" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.E4Xa" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E4Xa.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle+" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>+</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle+</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E4Xa.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle w_{\text{ref}}\left(d_{\text{ref},t-1}-d_{\text{ref},t}\right)\,\mathbb{I}[g_{t}=1]," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>w</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>ref</mtext></msub><mo>(</mo><mi>d</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mtext>ref</mtext><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>d</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mtext>ref</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo rspace="0.170em">)</mo><mi>𝕀</mi><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>g</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle w_{\text{ref}}\left(d_{\text{ref},t-1}-d_{\text{ref},t}\right)\,\mathbb{I}[g_{t}=1],</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p4.6" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{t}\in\{0,1\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{t}\in\{0,1\}</annotation></semantics></math> is a phase gate within each stage: <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{t}{=}0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{t}{=}0</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the reach phase and <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{t}{=}1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{t}{=}1</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the place phase, switching to <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m21" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math> at the reach event. The distances are defined as
<math id="S3.SS2.p4.m22" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{\text{rbt},t}=\lVert\mathbf{p}_{\text{rbt},t}-\mathbf{p}_{\text{act},t}\rVert_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mrow><mtext>rbt</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo rspace="0.1389em">=</mo><msub><mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0.1389em" rspace="0em">∥</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐩</mi><mrow><mtext>rbt</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝐩</mi><mrow><mtext>act</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em">∥</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{\text{rbt},t}=\lVert\mathbf{p}_{\text{rbt},t}-\mathbf{p}_{\text{act},t}\rVert_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>
and
<math id="S3.SS2.p4.m23" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{\text{ref},t}=\lVert\mathbf{p}_{\text{act},t}-\mathbf{p}_{\text{ref},t}\rVert_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mrow><mtext>ref</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo rspace="0.1389em">=</mo><msub><mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0.1389em" rspace="0em">∥</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐩</mi><mrow><mtext>act</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝐩</mi><mrow><mtext>ref</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em">∥</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{\text{ref},t}=\lVert\mathbf{p}_{\text{act},t}-\mathbf{p}_{\text{ref},t}\rVert_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>,
with weights <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m24" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(w_{\text{rbt}},w_{\text{ref}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mtext>rbt</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mtext>ref</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(w_{\text{rbt}},w_{\text{ref}})</annotation></semantics></math>.
(3) <span id="S3.SS2.p4.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Smoothness</span>: we penalize sudden changes between consecutive actions to smooth the policy output. (4) <span id="S3.SS2.p4.6.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Slowdown Near Target</span>: we encourage the object to settle by rewarding low object speed when it is close to the reference target. Full definitions and hyperparameters are provided in the supplementary materials.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Termination</span>.
(1) Task success: The episode terminates upon task success; We also apply early-termination conditions to improve training stability and prune unproductive explorations:
(2) Outside: the robot moves outside a predefined world box;
(3) Collision: an obstacle is collided with by the robot or the active box.
We avoid a dense collision penalty to avoid reward hacking and tedious weight tuning;
early termination
truncates future returns and thus provides a strong negative signal;
(4) Time limit: <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> in Eq. <a href="#S3.E2" title="In III-B Phase 1 (Teacher): Online Reinforcement Learning ‣ III Method ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> reaches its budget <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T_{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T_{s}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">EgoPush-Teacher</span>.
We use a PointNet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>]</cite> as the teacher state estimator. Due to occlusions and FOV cropping, the number of visible points varies over time;
PointNet handles variable-sized point sets via a shared per-point MLP and symmetric pooling, making it permutation-invariant.
At time <math id="S3.SS2.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, let <math id="S3.SS2.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{t}^{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>P</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{t}^{k}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the visible point set of semantic group <math id="S3.SS2.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k\in\{\mathrm{act},\mathrm{anc},\mathrm{obs},\mathrm{ref}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mi>act</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>anc</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>obs</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ref</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k\in\{\mathrm{act},\mathrm{anc},\mathrm{obs},\mathrm{ref}\}</annotation></semantics></math>. We encode each group into a group-wise latent <math id="S3.SS2.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z_{t}^{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>Z</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z_{t}^{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S3.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z_{t}^{k}=\mathrm{PointNet}_{\theta}(P_{t}^{k}),\quad k\in\{\mathrm{act},\,\mathrm{anc},\,\mathrm{obs},\,\mathrm{ref}\}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>Z</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>PointNet</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>P</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mi>act</mi><mo rspace="0.337em">,</mo><mi>anc</mi><mo rspace="0.337em">,</mo><mi>obs</mi><mo rspace="0.337em">,</mo><mi>ref</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z_{t}^{k}=\mathrm{PointNet}_{\theta}(P_{t}^{k}),\quad k\in\{\mathrm{act},\,\mathrm{anc},\,\mathrm{obs},\,\mathrm{ref}\}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p6.2" class="ltx_p">We then pass them together with the previous action <math id="S3.SS2.p6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{t-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{t-1}</annotation></semantics></math> to a MLP:</p>
<table id="S3.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{t}=\mathrm{MLP}\!\left(a_{t-1},\,Z_{t}^{\mathrm{act}},\,Z_{t}^{\mathrm{anc}},\,Z_{t}^{\mathrm{obs}},\,Z_{t}^{\mathrm{ref}}\right)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mpadded style="width:2.371em;" width="2.371em"><mi>MLP</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>Z</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>act</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>Z</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>anc</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>Z</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>obs</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>Z</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>ref</mi></msubsup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{t}=\mathrm{MLP}\!\left(a_{t-1},\,Z_{t}^{\mathrm{act}},\,Z_{t}^{\mathrm{anc}},\,Z_{t}^{\mathrm{obs}},\,Z_{t}^{\mathrm{ref}}\right).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p6.3" class="ltx_p">We train the teacher policy using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>]</cite> and apply domain randomization to key physical parameters.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S3.SS3.6" class="ltx_text">III-C</span> </span><span id="S3.SS3.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Phase 2 (Student): Supervised Learning</span></h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Observation</span>.
The student is equipped with an egocentric RGB-D camera. RGB is used only to obtain instance masks for semantic grouping while the policy network takes depth-only inputs.
Specifically, we run instance-level segmentation <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{inst}(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{inst}(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> on the RGB image <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I_{t}^{\mathrm{rgb}}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times 3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>I</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>rgb</mi></msubsup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>W</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I_{t}^{\mathrm{rgb}}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times 3}</annotation></semantics></math> to obtain a binary mask <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{t}^{(i)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>M</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{t}^{(i)}</annotation></semantics></math> for each visible object instance <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>,
and assign each instance to a semantic group <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{I}_{t}^{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{I}_{t}^{k}</annotation></semantics></math>, based on its task role (active / anchor / obstacle).
We then apply these masks to the depth map <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times 1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>W</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times 1}</annotation></semantics></math> and aggregate instances within each group by pixel-wise summation, producing three fixed-dimensional depth layers <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{d}_{t}^{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>d</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>t</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{d}_{t}^{k}</annotation></semantics></math>, as shown in Fig. <a href="#S3.F1" title="Fig. 1 ‣ III-B Phase 1 (Teacher): Online Reinforcement Learning ‣ III Method ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>:</p>
<table id="S3.E7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{M_{t}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{N_{t}}=S_{\text{inst}}(I_{t}^{\mathrm{rgb}})," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msubsup><mi>M</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mtext>inst</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>I</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>rgb</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{M_{t}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{N_{t}}=S_{\text{inst}}(I_{t}^{\mathrm{rgb}}),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
