</table>
<table id="S3.E9" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{d}_{t}^{k}=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{t}^{k}}\tilde{d}_{t}^{(i)},\quad\forall k\in\{\mathrm{act},\mathrm{anc},\mathrm{obs}\}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>d</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>t</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>∈</mo><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup></mrow></munder><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>d</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∀</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>act</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>anc</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>obs</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{d}_{t}^{k}=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{t}^{k}}\tilde{d}_{t}^{(i)},\quad\forall k\in\{\mathrm{act},\mathrm{anc},\mathrm{obs}\},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(9)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is the number of visible instances at time <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Since instance masks <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{M_{t}^{(i)}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msubsup><mi>M</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{M_{t}^{(i)}\}</annotation></semantics></math> are spatially disjoint, the summation in Eq. <a href="#S3.E9" title="In III-C Phase 2 (Student): Supervised Learning ‣ III Method ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> aggregates all instances within the same semantic category into a single depth layer <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{d}_{t}^{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>d</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>t</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{d}_{t}^{k}</annotation></semantics></math> without pixel-wise interference,
ensuring a constant input dimensionality for the visual backbone.
Recent progress in zero-shot segmentation models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>, <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>]</cite> suggests that obtaining such masks from RGB can be reliable in real scenes;
however, to focus on the core problems, we use color-coded objects and HSV-threshold segmentation in our experiments (see Appendix <a href="#S4a" title="D Image Processing ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a>).
We further address the sim-to-real gap of depth by simulating the noise pattern when training and applying the Navier-Stokes inpainting algorithm <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>, <a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite> to denoise in real world.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">EgoPush-Student</span>.
For the student, we use a CNN as the state estimator to encode the masked depth for each semantic group;
the rest of the network architecture is kept the same as the teacher (i.e., the same MLP policy head):</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S3.E10" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{Z}_{t}^{k}=\mathrm{CNN}_{\phi}\!\left(\tilde{d}_{t}^{k}\right),\quad k\in\{\mathrm{act},\mathrm{anc},\mathrm{obs}\}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>CNN</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>d</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>t</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>act</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>anc</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>obs</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{Z}_{t}^{k}=\mathrm{CNN}_{\phi}\!\left(\tilde{d}_{t}^{k}\right),\quad k\in\{\mathrm{act},\mathrm{anc},\mathrm{obs}\},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(10)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<table id="S3.E11" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{a}_{t}=\mathrm{MLP}\!\left(a_{t-1},\,\hat{Z}_{t}^{\mathrm{act}},\,\hat{Z}_{t}^{\mathrm{anc}},\,\hat{Z}_{t}^{\mathrm{obs}}\right)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>a</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mpadded style="width:2.371em;" width="2.371em"><mi>MLP</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi><mi>act</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi><mi>anc</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi><mi>obs</mi></msubsup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{a}_{t}=\mathrm{MLP}\!\left(a_{t-1},\,\hat{Z}_{t}^{\mathrm{act}},\,\hat{Z}_{t}^{\mathrm{anc}},\,\hat{Z}_{t}^{\mathrm{obs}}\right).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(11)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We avoid pure BC to minimize the mean squared error (MSE) between student and teacher actions, because contact-rich tasks such as pushing are extremely sensitive to closed-loop errors:
once the student exhibits a small deviation early on, subsequent states quickly drift away from the teacher’s demonstration distribution, making pure BC difficult to recover;
instead, we adopt an online DAgger-style distillation procedure: in each iteration,
we query the teacher online at the currently visited states to produce action labels, and the student immediately performs one supervised parameter update.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Beyond supervised action cloning, we introduce a relational distillation loss to bridge the representation gap between the privileged PointNet-based teacher and the vision-based student.
Given the teacher’s latent space contains a privileged reference embedding <math id="S3.SS3.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z_{t}^{\text{ref}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>Z</mi><mi>t</mi><mtext>ref</mtext></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z_{t}^{\text{ref}}</annotation></semantics></math>,
whereas the student must operate solely on egocentric observations <math id="S3.SS3.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\hat{Z}_{t}^{\text{act}},\hat{Z}_{t}^{\text{anc}},\hat{Z}_{t}^{\text{obs}}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi><mtext>act</mtext></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi><mtext>anc</mtext></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi><mtext>obs</mtext></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\hat{Z}_{t}^{\text{act}},\hat{Z}_{t}^{\text{anc}},\hat{Z}_{t}^{\text{obs}}\}</annotation></semantics></math> without explicit target indicators.
Due to this dimensional and structural misalignment, a direct global MSE loss between the teacher and student latent spaces is mathematically ill-defined.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p7.1" class="ltx_p">To bridge this gap, we propose to align the invariant relational structure between the common semantic entities.
Since the relative pose between the anchor and the reference target is invariant across episodes of the same task category, the student policy does not require an explicit goal observation.
We compute the pairwise cosine similarity matrix <math id="S3.SS3.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐒</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{S}</annotation></semantics></math> for the shared groups <math id="S3.SS3.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{K}_{\text{shared}}=\{\mathrm{act,anc,obs}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒦</mi><mtext>shared</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mi>act</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>anc</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>obs</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{K}_{\text{shared}}=\{\mathrm{act,anc,obs}\}</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S3.E12" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E12.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{i,j}=\frac{Z^{i}\cdot Z^{j}}{\|Z^{i}\|_{2}\|Z^{j}\|_{2}},\quad i,j\in\mathcal{K}_{\text{shared}}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>Z</mi><mi>i</mi></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msup><mi>Z</mi><mi>j</mi></msup></mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msup><mi>Z</mi><mi>i</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msup><mi>Z</mi><mi>j</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒦</mi><mtext>shared</mtext></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{i,j}=\frac{Z^{i}\cdot Z^{j}}{\|Z^{i}\|_{2}\|Z^{j}\|_{2}},\quad i,j\in\mathcal{K}_{\text{shared}},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(12)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p8.1" class="ltx_p">By minimizing <math id="S3.SS3.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{rel}}=\|\mathbf{S}_{t}^{\text{tea}}-\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{t}^{\text{stu}}\|_{F}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>rel</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐒</mi><mi>t</mi><mtext>tea</mtext></msubsup><mo>−</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐒</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi><mtext>stu</mtext></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{rel}}=\|\mathbf{S}_{t}^{\text{tea}}-\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{t}^{\text{stu}}\|_{F}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, we force the student to mimic the teacher’s perception of relative spatial configurations.
Crucially, although the student lacks the explicit <math id="S3.SS3.p8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z_{t}^{\text{ref}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>Z</mi><mi>t</mi><mtext>ref</mtext></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z_{t}^{\text{ref}}</annotation></semantics></math>, it learns to satisfy the task objective by inheriting the teacher’s refined understanding of the active-anchor-obstacle relationship,
which implicitly encodes the target-seeking behavior demonstrated by the teacher.
We warm-start the student by initializing the MLP policy network with the teacher’s learned weights, so the student trains from an informed prior rather than from scratch, substantially accelerating convergence.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p9.1" class="ltx_p">During distillation, beyond the physical-parameter randomization in Phase 1, we further apply domain randomization to camera-pose-related observations to improve the student’s robustness during real-world deployment.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">IV </span><span id="S4.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Experiments</span></h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate EgoPush in both simulation and real-world and demonstrate that:
(1) Our method achieves precise multi-object rearrangement for items with diverse geometries into various target formations in both simulation and real world, as shown in Fig. <span class="ltx_ref ltx_missing_label ltx_ref_self"></span>;
(2) Restricting Observation Space for RL Teacher ensures that the student receives a more accessible and distillable supervision signal, leading to superior performance;
(3) Decomposing long-horizon tasks into sequential sub-tasks and employing time-decayed task completion rewards at the stage level significantly accelerates RL convergence;
(4) Incorporating an auxiliary Relational Distillation loss enables the student to effectively inherit the teacher’s spatial reasoning.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S4.SS1.6" class="ltx_text">IV-A</span> </span><span id="S4.SS1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Experimental Setup</span></h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The RL policy is trained in NVIDIA Isaac Lab. We utilize an AMD EPYC Turin 9355 CPU and an NVIDIA RTX A6000 Ada GPU for both RL training and policy distillation. During the RL phase, we deploy 8,192 parallel environments for training, while the distillation phase employs 512 parallel environments for online supervised learning. In simulation, the manipulated objects consist of three primitive shapes: a cube (<math id="S4.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="15\times 15\times 15" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>15</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>15</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>15</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">15\times 15\times 15</annotation></semantics></math> cm), a cylinder (diameter <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="15" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>15</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">15</annotation></semantics></math> cm, height <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="15" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>15</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">15</annotation></semantics></math> cm), and a triangular prism (equilateral base with <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="15" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>15</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">15</annotation></semantics></math> cm side length, height <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="15" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>15</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">15</annotation></semantics></math> cm). The robot’s collision body is modeled as a <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="14\times 14\times 14.3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>14</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>14</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>14.3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">14\times 14\times 14.3</annotation></semantics></math> cm cube. To account for the minimum depth sensing range of approximately <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="15" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>15</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">15</annotation></semantics></math> cm of the real-world camera, we equipped the robot with a pusher of <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="7.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>7.5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">7.5</annotation></semantics></math> cm length. We utilize an RGB-D camera with a <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="69^{\circ}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>69</mn><mo>∘</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">69^{\circ}</annotation></semantics></math> horizontal Field of View (FOV) and a resolution of <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="240\times 180" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>240</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>180</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">240\times 180</annotation></semantics></math> pixels.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">From our designed tasks (Fig.  <span class="ltx_ref ltx_missing_label ltx_ref_self"></span>), we initially utilize a relatively straightforward cross-shaped formation task involving cubes. The ablated components already exhibit a significant performance gap compared to our full method.
Consequently, we adopt this task as the standard evaluation benchmark for the first two distillation experiments.
During testing, the teacher model performs across 1,024 episodes, while the student model is tested across 256 episodes.
We further evaluate our model on objects with different geometries in appendix <a href="#S5.SS1" title="E.1 Different Boxes shapes ‣ E Additional Experiment Results ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.1</span></a>.
However, for the Relational Distillation ablation, the ablated version achieves performance comparable to our model on the cross-shape task.
To further differentiate their capabilities, we introduce a more challenging line-shape formation task.
Finally, for baseline comparisons, we simplify the environment to a two-object setup where the goal is to push one object towards another.
Even in this simplified scenario, the baselines perform poorly, failing to yield satisfactory results.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S4.SS2.6" class="ltx_text">IV-B</span> </span><span id="S4.SS2.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Ablation Studies</span></h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Restricted Observations for RL Teacher</span>.
We constrain the RL teacher’s observations to mitigate the observability mismatch between the privileged teacher and the partially-observed student. This approach incorporates two key designs: virtual egocentric FOV masking and center-gated visibility for privileged reference keypoints. To evaluate the efficacy of these designs, we consider two relaxed teacher variants: 
<br class="ltx_break">(i) <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">w/o FOV Masking (global)</span>, which removes the virtual egocentric FOV constraint and exposes global keypoints; and (ii)<span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> w/o Center-Gated Visibility (w/o C-GV)</span>, which retains the FOV but removes the center-gated reference visibility.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S4.T1.8" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">TABLE I</span>: </span><span id="S4.T1.9" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Ablation Studies of RL teacher observations. <span id="S4.T1.9.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SR</span> denotes success rate, <span id="S4.T1.9.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ExecTime</span> denotes execution time per episode, and <span id="S4.T1.9.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">TrajLen</span> denotes trajectory length. The <span id="S4.T1.9.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ExecTime</span> and <span id="S4.T1.9.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">TrajLen</span> are only computed for successful episodes.</span></figcaption>

</table>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">All teacher variants are trained with the same reinforcement learning algorithm, reward functions, and hyperparameters, and are distilled into students with the same visual architecture. Furthermore, all policies are trained for a sufficiently extensive duration to ensure full convergence.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="TABLE I ‣ IV-B Ablation Studies ‣ IV Experiments ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">I</span></a> reports teacher and student performance together with metrics for the above variants.
Analysis of the results in the table reveals that the Teacher Success Rate (SR) remains consistently high across all three settings (<math id="S4.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&gt;98\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&gt;</mo><mrow><mn>98</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&gt;98\%</annotation></semantics></math>), validating the soundness of our reinforcement learning framework.
In terms of execution time and trajectory length, the Global setting significantly outperforms the other two, while the w/o C-GV variant is slightly better than our policy. This trend is expected: as the teacher’s observations become more constrained, its performance degrades accordingly.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">However, the student results tell a drastically different story. The w/o C-GV variant attains only a 21% success rate, whereas our student reaches 70%. Even though the Global teacher is near-perfect, its student fails to achieve a single successful episode. For execution time and trajectory length (computed over successful episodes only), w/o C-GV appears shorter than our student. This is mainly due to a success-selection effect: w/o C-GV succeeds only on trivial instances (<em id="S4.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">e.g</em>.<span id="S4.SS2.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text"></span>, the active object starts close to and already facing the anchor), which naturally yield short trajectories. Our student succeeds on harder instances that require longer navigation and pushing, thereby increasing the mean ExecTime and trajectory length among successful runs.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F2" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">

</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_3">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F2.sf3.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">(c)</span> </span><span id="S4.F2.sf3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">w/o FOV(global)</span></figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Fig. 2</span>: </span><span id="S4.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Comparative analysis of teacher observation spaces.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">To provide an intuitive explanation for the observed teacher–student capability misalignment, Fig. <a href="#S4.F2" title="Fig. 2 ‣ IV-B Ablation Studies ‣ IV Experiments ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> visualizes the teacher behaviors under the three observation settings.
Under our setting, the teacher predominantly pushes while facing the anchor to keep it within the gated FOV, thereby maintaining visibility of the C-GV–constrained reference point cloud (Fig. <a href="#S4.F2.sf1" title="In Fig. 2 ‣ IV-B Ablation Studies ‣ IV Experiments ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2(a)</span></a>);
In contrast, the w/o C-GV teacher often sees only a partial set of the anchor keypoints and effectively follows a ‘lazy’ strategy that tracks the reference point cloud without explicitly controlling anchor visibility; consequently, the student receives sparse actionable cues and fails to recover the teacher’s performance (Fig. <a href="#S4.F2.sf2" title="In Fig. 2 ‣ IV-B Ablation Studies ‣ IV Experiments ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2(b)</span></a>);
Under Global observation, the teacher is unconstrained and frequently pushes while facing away from the anchor, producing behaviors that are fundamentally not learnable from the student’s egocentric observations (Fig. <a href="#S4.F2.sf3" title="In Fig. 2 ‣ IV-B Ablation Studies ‣ IV Experiments ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2(c)</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Credit Assignment Ablation.</span>
To validate the learning difficulty of the long-horizon sequential rearrangement task and to assess the effectiveness of our credit-assignment design, we ablate the reward shaping components used for credit assignment in a progressive manner.
Starting from a sparse baseline (<span id="S4.SS2.p6.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Base</span>) that provides only episode-terminal success feedback, we introduce stage-wise rewards computed per stage (<span id="S4.SS2.p6.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SWR</span>) to encourage sub-goal attainment, using the reaching and placing terms in Eq. <a href="#S3.E1" title="In III-B Phase 1 (Teacher): Online Reinforcement Learning ‣ III Method ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> and Eq. <a href="#S3.E3" title="In III-B Phase 1 (Teacher): Online Reinforcement Learning ‣ III Method ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> without the temporal decay factor in Eq. <a href="#S3.E2" title="In III-B Phase 1 (Teacher): Online Reinforcement Learning ‣ III Method ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. We then add temporal decay based on a global episode timer (<span id="S4.SS2.p6.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SWR+TD</span>) by applying Eq. <a href="#S3.E2" title="In III-B Phase 1 (Teacher): Online Reinforcement Learning ‣ III Method ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> with episode-level timing. Finally, <span id="S4.SS2.p6.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ours</span> uses a stage timer that resets the decay schedule at each stage boundary, so that each stage receives comparable temporal pressure.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p7.1" class="ltx_p">The training curves (Fig. <a href="#S4.F3" title="Fig. 3 ‣ IV-B Ablation Studies ‣ IV Experiments ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>) show that <span id="S4.SS2.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ours</span> converges faster and more stably, suggesting that stage-aligned temporal shaping provides a more consistent learning signal across sequential stages.
<span id="S4.SS2.p7.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">This comparison uses an unmatched training budget</span>: <span id="S4.SS2.p7.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ours</span> is trained only until it has largely converged (about <math id="S4.SS2.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>45k steps), whereas to better isolate the effect of individual ablated components,
we continue training the other variants for an additional steps, resulting in a total of <math id="S4.SS2.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>90k steps. We report results using the best checkpoint achieved by each variant under its respective training budget.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p8.1" class="ltx_p">Quantitative results are reported in Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="TABLE II ‣ IV-B Ablation Studies ‣ IV Experiments ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">II</span></a>. <em id="S4.SS2.p8.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Base</em> learns unreliably in this long-horizon setting, indicating that sparse terminal feedback is inadequate for temporal credit assignment. Adding stage-wise rewards (<em id="S4.SS2.p8.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">SWR</em>) substantially improves learnability, highlighting the benefit of stage decomposition. Introducing temporal decay with an episode-level timer (<em id="S4.SS2.p8.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">SWR+TD</em>) further boosts performance, especially success rate, by encouraging earlier, decision-critical actions. Finally, <span id="S4.SS2.p8.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ours</span> reaches near-saturated performance by resetting the decay schedule at each stage boundary with a stage timer—<span id="S4.SS2.p8.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">despite using only half the training steps</span>, underscoring its more effective long-horizon credit assignment.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T2" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S4.T2.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">TABLE II</span>: </span><span id="S4.T2.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Credit assignment ablation on Cross Rearrangement Task.Starting from an episode-terminal reward baseline, we progressively add stage-wise rewards(<span id="S4.T2.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SWR</span>),
temporal decay using a global episode timer (<span id="S4.T2.7.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">TD</span>), and a stage timer (<span id="S4.T2.7.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ST</span>) that resets the
decay schedule at stage boundaries.
</span></figcaption>

<figure id="S4.F3" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18071v1/cross_train_curves_50k_side_by_side.svg" id="S4.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/195;" width="476" height="195"></object>

<div id="S4.SS2.p9" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p9.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p9.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Relational Distillation Ablation</span>.
To evaluate the effect of relational supervision, we ablate the additional supervision in Eq. <a href="#S3.E12" title="In III-C Phase 2 (Student): Supervised Learning ‣ III Method ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a> and perform distillation with action loss only (<em id="S4.SS2.p9.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">w/o Relational Distillation</em>). In <span id="S4.SS2.p9.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Cross</span>, the student remains competitive with <span id="S4.SS2.p9.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ours</span>, likely because the anchor is fixed and the per-stage spatial relations are close to symmetric. However, <span id="S4.SS2.p9.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Line-Shape</span> is more sensitive: small errors compound over the sequential execution, and the target configuration is not symmetric. Under this setting, <em id="S4.SS2.p9.1.6" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">w/o Relational Distillation</em> yields a noticeably larger converged action loss and completely fails in final performance (Fig. <a href="#S4.F4" title="Fig. 4 ‣ IV-B Ablation Studies ‣ IV Experiments ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F4" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18071v1/distill_train_raw_action_loss_curve.svg" id="S4.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:333/253;" width="333" height="253"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F4.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Fig. 4</span>: </span><span id="S4.F4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Distillation training curve for distillation ablation.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S4.SS3.6" class="ltx_text">IV-C</span> </span><span id="S4.SS3.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Baseline Comparisons</span></h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To demonstrate the difficulty of our task setting and the effectiveness of EgoPush, we compare against both a classical mapping-based baseline and a suite of end-to-end (E2E) deep reinforcement learning baselines with different observation modalities.
Specifically, we include a traditional approach based on spatial intention maps <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>]</cite>, as well as E2E visual RL variants that use RGB, RGB-D, oracle semantic masks (RGBD-Sem), and recurrent policies (RGBD-RNN).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We include Spatial Intention Maps (SIM) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>]</cite> as a representative classical mapping-and-planning baseline. To align with our egocentric setup, we construct a 2D top-down semantic map from egocentric ground truth (<em id="S4.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">GT</em>) RGB-D observations with <em id="S4.SS3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">GT</em> segmentation for semantics (to avoid confounding SIM with perception errors). For fairness, we do not provide robot ground-truth pose; instead, SIM uses an odometry-style pose obtained by integrating the <em id="S4.SS3.p2.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">executed</em> local velocities, which may drift over long-horizon, contact-rich episodes and degrade map consistency. SIM outputs a local spatial target (pixel/waypoint), which we convert to the same local velocity action interface via a waypoint-tracking controller with identical action bounds.
For RGBD-Sem, we assume perfect semantic segmentation and provide the ground-truth mask together with depth as input.
All learning-based methods are trained from scratch using the same reward definition, termination conditions, and training budget.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="TABLE III ‣ IV-C Baseline Comparisons ‣ IV Experiments ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">III</span></a> summarizes the comparative results.
Across all E2E variants, learning from egocentric observations remains brittle: although several baselines achieve non-trivial <span id="S4.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Reach</span>, their success rates remains below 1%, indicating a failure to complete the long-horizon push-and-align objective.
Notably, even with GT semantic masks, RGBD-Sem still fails to solve the task, suggesting that perfect object-level perception alone does not resolve the underlying difficulty.
These results point to long-horizon geometric reasoning and maintaining spatial consistency under partial observability as the dominant bottlenecks, especially when contact-rich interactions perturb object configurations and key objects may temporarily leave the FOV.
SIM also performs poorly: without GT pose, action-integrated odometry drift accumulates over long horizons and undermines mapping and planning consistency, leading to compounding errors in dynamic, contact-rich scenes.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In contrast, EgoPush achieves a success rate of 100% with 100% reach rate, demonstrating robust long-horizon capability under the same egocentric sensing constraints.
These results support our central claim that visually grounded distillation and structured supervision are crucial for solving long-horizon, contact-rich rearrangement from egocentric vision. We provide qualitative analyses of representative success and failure cases in the appendix <a href="#S1a" title="A Qualitative Analysis of Baseline Policies ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T3" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S4.T3.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">TABLE III</span>: </span><span id="S4.T3.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Baseline comparisons on a simplified task.<span id="S4.T3.8.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">
We report reached the active object rate (</span>Reach<span id="S4.T3.8.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">), Success Rate (</span>SR<span id="S4.T3.8.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">; counted as place the active object near anchor), and Trajectory Length (</span>Traj<span id="S4.T3.8.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">) for successful episodes.</span></span></figcaption>
<div id="S4.T3.9" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_center ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:345.0pt;height:130.7pt;vertical-align:-63.5pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(11.4pt,-4.3pt) scale(1.07094198704255,1.07094198704255) ;">
<table id="S4.T3.9.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="S4.T3.9.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S4.T3.9.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_tt" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;"><span id="S4.T3.9.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:70%;">Method</span></th>
<th id="S4.T3.9.1.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_tt" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;"><span id="S4.T3.9.1.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:70%;">Input</span></th>

<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S4.SS4.6" class="ltx_text">IV-D</span> </span><span id="S4.SS4.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Real World Experiments</span></h3>

<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Real world experiments are conducted in a <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3\text{m}\times 3\text{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>m</mtext></mrow><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>m</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3\text{m}\times 3\text{m}</annotation></semantics></math> arena(shown in the left of Fig. <span class="ltx_ref ltx_missing_label ltx_ref_self"></span>), containing a single mobile robot (TurtleBot3 Burger) equipped with an Intel RealSense D435i camera and multiple boxes of distinct colors. The arena floor is gray and surrounded by foam walls of the same color to facilitate segmentation of the boxes. The boxes are <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="15\text{cm}\times 15\text{cm}\times 15\text{cm}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><mn>15</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>cm</mtext></mrow><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>15</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>cm</mtext></mrow><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>15</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>cm</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">15\text{cm}\times 15\text{cm}\times 15\text{cm}</annotation></semantics></math> cubes covered with colored paper. At the beginning of each trial, the robot and all boxes are placed with random initial positions and orientations inside the arena. Fig. <a href="#S4.F5" title="Fig. 5 ‣ IV-D Real World Experiments ‣ IV Experiments ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> visualizes the experiment setup and robot configuration. The onboard Jetson Nano transmits captured RGB-D frames to a remote RTX 5080 server via WebSocket, which performs real-time policy computation and returns control signals to the robot’s low-level controller.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F5" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18071v1/hardware_setup.png" id="S4.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:429/259;" width="429" height="259" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F5.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Fig. 5</span>: </span><span id="S4.F5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Real-world hardware setup.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We zero-shot deployed the best student policy into this real-world setup and tested 10 episodes of the cross-shape task with 5 boxes. The real robot was able to finish pushing all four boxes to the anchor box within 2 minutes, achieving an 80 % success rate under a loose evaluation metric (allowing for minor orientation and centering deviations). In general, we observed that the policy behavior was qualitatively similar to that in simulation. However, the policy’s action scale was restricted to accommodate the servo torque limits of the real robot, resulting in a slight degradation of task robustness and efficiency in training in simulation.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">V </span><span id="S5.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Discussions</span></h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we presented <span id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">EgoPush</span>, a framework that enables mobile robots to solve long-horizon multi-object rearrangement tasks using solely egocentric vision.
While our constrained teacher and structured supervision substantially improve distillability and robustness, several limitations remain and motivate future work.
Our student is primarily reactive: it conditions on the current egocentric observation (group-wise depth) and a short action history, but does not maintain an explicit belief over objects that are temporarily unobserved. In scenes with <em id="S5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">consecutive</em> obstacles, we observe a characteristic dilemma: facing the goal (anchor/target cues) can occlude the feasible corridor, while turning to inspect a feasible corridor may lose goal cues altogether. Without memory, the policy can enter an oscillatory or deadlock mode—alternating between “goal-seeking” and “path-seeking” views without committing to a globally consistent maneuver. This failure mode is especially pronounced when the robot must thread through narrow passages while continuously coordinating contact with the active object.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Importantly, our object-centric latent interface suggests a promising direction to mitigate this limitation: leveraging the latent space as a compact spatial state and integrating it with recurrent sequence models (<em id="S5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">e.g</em>.<span id="S5.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text"></span>, GRU/LSTM) to learn <em id="S5.p2.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">spatial memory</em>. Since the latent features are structured around task roles and encode relative relations rather than absolute poses, they provide a natural substrate for temporal aggregation across occlusions, enabling the agent to maintain a persistent belief over traversable corridors and goal cues even when either becomes temporarily out of view.</p>
</div>
</section>

<section id="S1a" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">A </span><span id="S1a.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Qualitative Analysis of Baseline Policies</span></h2>

<div id="S1a.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1a.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This section documents qualitative failure modes observed in our baseline comparisons. We first summarize the <span id="S1a.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">shared training protocol and timing</span> used for all baselines, and then analyze representative failure cases.</p>
</div>
<section id="S1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.1 </span><span id="S1.SS1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Shared Training Protocol and Timing (Fairness)</span></h3>

<div id="S1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">All learning-based baselines reported in Section <a href="#S4.SS3" title="IV-C Baseline Comparisons ‣ IV Experiments ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">IV-C</span></a> (Baseline Comparisons), Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="TABLE III ‣ IV-C Baseline Comparisons ‣ IV Experiments ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">III</span></a> of the main manuscript are trained from scratch under identical simulator timing, action bounds, and interaction budget. Concretely, the physics time step is fixed at <math id="S1.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1/60\,\text{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>60</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>s</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1/60\,\text{s}</annotation></semantics></math> and actions are applied with a decimation of <math id="S1.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="6" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>6</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">6</annotation></semantics></math>, so each policy step corresponds to <math id="S1.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.1\,\text{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.1</mn><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>s</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.1\,\text{s}</annotation></semantics></math> of simulated time (<math id="S1.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10\,\text{Hz}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>Hz</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10\,\text{Hz}</annotation></semantics></math> control). Unless explicitly stated, we keep the same termination conditions and total PPO training budget across E2E variants; the primary differences are the observation modality (RGB, RGB-D, or oracle semantics) and the policy backbone (feed-forward or recurrent). For the SIM baseline, we follow the original observation-space design <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>]</cite>, using a map-based observation, a spatial waypoint action, and a SIM-style reward composed of progress, success, and collision-penalty terms. Table <a href="#S1.T4" title="TABLE IV ‣ A.1 Shared Training Protocol and Timing (Fairness) ‣ A Qualitative Analysis of Baseline Policies ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">IV</span></a> lists the full reproducibility settings.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.T4" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S1.T4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">TABLE IV</span>: </span><span id="S1.T4.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Reproducibility details for baseline comparisons for Section <a href="#S4.SS3" title="IV-C Baseline Comparisons ‣ IV Experiments ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">IV-C</span></a> (Baseline Comparisons), Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="TABLE III ‣ IV-C Baseline Comparisons ‣ IV Experiments ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">III</span></a> in the main manuscript.<span id="S1.T4.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">
All baselines share the same environment timing, action bounds, and PPO hyperparameters. E2E baselines use the same reward set, with an optional two-stage curriculum schedule, while the SIM baseline uses a SIM-style reward and waypoint macro-actions.</span></span></figcaption>
<table id="S1.T4.6" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_align_middle">

<td id="S1.T5.7.6.5.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left" style="padding:0.7pt 2.0pt;"><span id="S1.T5.7.6.5.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Policy directly predicts </span><math id="S1.T5.m33" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(v,\omega)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">v</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">ω</mi><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(v,\omega)</annotation></semantics></math></td></tr>
<tr id="S1.T5.7.6.5.1.2" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S1.T5.7.6.5.1.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left" style="padding:0.7pt 2.0pt;"><span id="S1.T5.7.6.5.1.2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">both channels normalized to </span><math id="S1.T5.m34" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[-1,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">−</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn></mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[-1,1]</annotation></semantics></math></td></tr>
</table></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S1.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.2 </span><span id="S1.SS2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">End-to-End Visual RL Baselines</span></h3>

<div id="S1.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Before analyzing qualitative failure cases, we briefly summarize the configuration differences among E2E baselines. All E2E variants are <span id="S1.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">visuomotor policies</span> that take egocentric observations and output <span id="S1.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">diff-drive</span> commands <math id="S1.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(v,\omega)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ω</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(v,\omega)</annotation></semantics></math>, without teacher supervision or explicit mapping. Concretely, <span id="S1.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">E2E-RGB</span> uses only ego RGB images; <span id="S1.SS2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">E2E-RGBD</span> additionally provides depth; <span id="S1.SS2.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">RGBD-Sem</span> augments RGB-D with <em id="S1.SS2.p1.1.6" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">oracle</em> semantic grouping via semantic patches and previous action input, to test whether explicit semantic segmentation alone is sufficient to solve the task; and <span id="S1.SS2.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">RGBD-RNN</span> adds a GRU head to test whether short-term memory alleviates partial observability. We further include an <span id="S1.SS2.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">E2E-Curriculum</span> variant trained in two stages: the first stage uses only reaching-related rewards (orientation, distance reduction, and touch), while goal-completion and safety terms are disabled; the second stage restores the full reward set for pushing and resumes from the first-stage checkpoint. The two stages use equal training budgets. We discuss the <span id="S1.SS2.p1.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SIM</span> map-based baseline separately in Sec. <a href="#S1.SS3" title="A.3 Spatial Intention Maps (SIM) Baseline ‣ A Qualitative Analysis of Baseline Policies ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.3</span></a>.
Across E2E variants (RGB, RGB-D, RGBD-Sem, and recurrent policies), the most salient limitation is <span id="S1.SS2.p1.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">short-horizon reactivity under partial observability</span>. Even when the agent transiently achieves the <em id="S1.SS2.p1.1.11" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Reach</em> event (touching the active box at least once), it often fails to maintain a stable interaction long enough to reliably transport the active box to the anchor region. We summarize several recurring failure patterns below.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(A) Control collapse: spinning in place or freezing.</span>
The most common degenerate outcome is that the robot either spins in place for the majority of the episode or remains nearly stationary after a brief initial motion. This behavior is consistent with the difficulty of long-horizon credit assignment from egocentric pixels: early in training, stochastic policies can occasionally obtain partial rewards by chance (e.g., briefly facing or touching the box), yet the resulting gradients may drive the policy toward a locally stable but task-irrelevant attractor.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(B) Early stopping before meaningful progress.</span>
We frequently observe policies that stop prematurely, either before making contact with the active box, or after pushing the box partway toward the goal but before satisfying the success condition. Qualitatively, this resembles learning a short-horizon sub-skill (e.g., approach or initiate pushing) without learning the full conditional logic required for completing the task (e.g., verifying box-at-goal and continuing to correct residual errors).</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(C) Goal chasing without contact (“pushing air”).</span>
Another common pattern is that the policy learns to orient toward the goal region (or the anchor) but fails to maintain contact with the active box. Once contact is lost, the robot continues to drive toward the goal as if the box were attached, effectively pushing empty space.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.SS2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(D) Premature pushing without reaching.</span>
Finally, some policies start executing push-like motions toward the goal without first reaching the active box, indicating that the policy has overfit to goal-directed cues while missing the prerequisite contact dynamics.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Even with <span id="S1.SS2.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">oracle semantic masks</span> (RGBD-Sem), performance remains poor. This indicates that <em id="S1.SS2.p6.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">recognizing</em> objects is not sufficient; what is missing is <span id="S1.SS2.p6.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">persistent spatial consistency</span>—the ability to remember where objects were, re-acquire them after occlusion, and coordinate navigation and pushing while the configuration changes. Representative E2E failure cases are shown in Figure <a href="#S1.F6" title="Fig. 6 ‣ A.4 Qualitative Visualizations ‣ A Qualitative Analysis of Baseline Policies ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> (first three rows).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S1.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.3 </span><span id="S1.SS3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Spatial Intention Maps (SIM) Baseline</span></h3>

<div id="S1.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">SIM represents a classical mapping-and-planning baseline built around a <span id="S1.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">map-centric</span> state representation and an explicit <span id="S1.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">spatial action</span> (selecting a target location on a map), rather than directly regressing low-level robot velocities from pixels. To adapt SIM to our benchmark, we retain its core ingredient—a robot-centric, heading-aligned <span id="S1.SS3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">spatial intention map</span>—as the policy input, and integrate it into our PPO pipeline. Concretely, we construct a local semantic map from oracle segmentation and let the policy output a waypoint <math id="S1.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(x,y)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x,y)</annotation></semantics></math> in the local map frame; a geometric controller then converts this waypoint into diff-drive commands <math id="S1.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(v,\omega)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ω</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(v,\omega)</annotation></semantics></math> under the same control rate and bounds as other baselines (Table <a href="#S1.T4" title="TABLE IV ‣ A.1 Shared Training Protocol and Timing (Fairness) ‣ A Qualitative Analysis of Baseline Policies ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">IV</span></a>). For training, we use a <span id="S1.SS3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SIM-style reward</span> consisting of a progress term (delta distance decrease), a sparse one-shot success term, and a lightweight collision penalty, matching the reward structure used in the original SIM work.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The main failure mode we observe is <span id="S1.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">state inconsistency caused by accumulated odometry and contact errors over time</span> (the real robot’s odometry drift is considerably worse than in simulation due to wheel slip, imperfect ground contact, and etc.). Since we do not provide GT robot pose, SIM updates its map using an odometry-style pose obtained by integrating <em id="S1.SS3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">executed</em> local velocities. Over long episodes, small integration errors accumulate; under repeated contacts, the discrepancy between assumed and true pose can grow large enough that the semantic map becomes misaligned with reality. This undermines both (i) local planning (targets chosen on a distorted map) and (ii) the feedback loop between map updates and action selection, yielding compounding errors.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In addition, the task requires <span id="S1.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">tight coupling between perception and interaction</span>. Even with a reasonably consistent map, pushing success depends on fine-grained alignment and maintaining stable contact, which is difficult to achieve with a purely map-based decision layer without structured, stage-aware supervision. In the supplementary videos, this often appears as repeated attempts to re-approach the active object or to push from unfavorable angles, leading to wasted steps and increased disturbances. Representative SIM failure cases are shown in Figure <a href="#S1.F6" title="Fig. 6 ‣ A.4 Qualitative Visualizations ‣ A Qualitative Analysis of Baseline Policies ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> (SIM-Odom row) and Figure <a href="#S1.F7" title="Fig. 7 ‣ A.4 Qualitative Visualizations ‣ A Qualitative Analysis of Baseline Policies ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>, where GT–map mismatch increases from left to right.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S1.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.4 </span><span id="S1.SS4.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Qualitative Visualizations</span></h3>

<div id="S1.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To make the above failure modes concrete, we provide <span id="S1.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">filmstrip-style qualitative case studies</span> over full episodes. Figure <a href="#S1.F6" title="Fig. 6 ‣ A.4 Qualitative Visualizations ‣ A Qualitative Analysis of Baseline Policies ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> summarizes four representative baseline failure patterns (three E2E rows and one SIM-Odom row), while Figure <a href="#S1.F7" title="Fig. 7 ‣ A.4 Qualitative Visualizations ‣ A Qualitative Analysis of Baseline Policies ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> shows a paired GT-vs-map sequence in which alignment degrades over time.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F6" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18071v1/Failure.png" id="S1.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/266;" width="476" height="266" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F6.8" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Fig. 6</span>: </span><span id="S1.F6.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Representative baseline failure filmstrips.<span id="S1.F6.9.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> From top to bottom: </span>E2E-RGBD<span id="S1.F6.9.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> collapses to a near-single action mode, </span>E2E-RNN<span id="S1.F6.9.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> exhibits premature termination, </span>E2E-Curriculum<span id="S1.F6.9.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> fails to maintain stable contact after initial approach, and </span>SIM-Odom<span id="S1.F6.9.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> shows incorrect interaction due to map/pose inconsistency.</span></span></figcaption>

</section>
</section>
<section id="S2a" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">B </span><span id="S2a.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Training Details</span></h2>

<section id="S2.SS1a" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.1 </span><span id="S2.SS1a.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Reward Function Details</span></h3>

<div id="S2.SS1a.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1a.p1.1" class="ltx_p">(3) <span id="S2.SS1a.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Smoothness</span>:
To smooth the output of the neural network, a penalty is implemented to discourage sudden changes by comparing the current action to the previous action:</p>
<table id="S2.E13" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E13.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="r_{\text{smooth},t}=(\Delta v_{t})^{4}\,\mathbb{I}\!\left[\Delta v_{t}&gt;\varepsilon_{\text{smooth}}\right]+(\Delta\omega_{t})^{4}\,\mathbb{I}\!\left[\Delta\omega_{t}&gt;\varepsilon_{\text{smooth}}\right]," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mtext>smooth</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>4</mn></msup><mpadded style="width:0.219em;" width="0.219em"><mi>𝕀</mi></mpadded><mrow><mo>[</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><msub><mi>ε</mi><mtext>smooth</mtext></msub><mo>]</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><msub><mi>ω</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>4</mn></msup><mpadded style="width:0.219em;" width="0.219em"><mi>𝕀</mi></mpadded><mrow><mo>[</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><msub><mi>ω</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><msub><mi>ε</mi><mtext>smooth</mtext></msub><mo>]</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{\text{smooth},t}=(\Delta v_{t})^{4}\,\mathbb{I}\!\left[\Delta v_{t}&gt;\varepsilon_{\text{smooth}}\right]+(\Delta\omega_{t})^{4}\,\mathbb{I}\!\left[\Delta\omega_{t}&gt;\varepsilon_{\text{smooth}}\right],</annotation></semantics></math></td>

</table>
<p id="S2.SS1a.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS1a.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS1a.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\omega_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ω</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\omega_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> are the linear and angular action components; <math id="S2.SS1a.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta v_{t}=v_{t}-v_{t-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta v_{t}=v_{t}-v_{t-1}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS1a.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta\omega_{t}=\omega_{t}-\omega_{t-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ω</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>ω</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>ω</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta\omega_{t}=\omega_{t}-\omega_{t-1}</annotation></semantics></math> denote consecutive action differences; <math id="S2.SS1a.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\varepsilon_{\text{smooth}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ε</mi><mtext>smooth</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varepsilon_{\text{smooth}}</annotation></semantics></math> is the (pre-scaling) threshold.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1a.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1a.p2.1" class="ltx_p">(4) <span id="S2.SS1a.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Slowdown Near Target</span>:</p>
<table id="S2.E14" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E14.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{\text{slow},t}=g_{d}(t)\,g_{v}(t)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mtext>slow</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>v</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{\text{slow},t}=g_{d}(t)\,g_{v}(t),</annotation></semantics></math></td>

</table>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1a.p3" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S2.E15" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E15.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="g_{d}(t)=\Bigg(1-\frac{\left\lVert\mathbf{p}_{\text{act},t}-\mathbf{p}_{\text{ref},t}\right\rVert_{2}}{\varepsilon_{d,\text{th}}}\Bigg)\mathbb{I}\!\left[\left\lVert\mathbf{p}_{\text{act},t}-\mathbf{p}_{\text{ref},t}\right\rVert_{2}&lt;\varepsilon_{d,\text{th}}\right]," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="2.600em" minsize="2.600em">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mfrac><msub><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐩</mi><mrow><mtext>act</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝐩</mi><mrow><mtext>ref</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><msub><mi>ε</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>th</mtext></mrow></msub></mfrac><mo maxsize="2.600em" minsize="2.600em">)</mo></mrow><mpadded style="width:0.219em;" width="0.219em"><mi>𝕀</mi></mpadded><mrow><mo>[</mo><msub><mrow><mo>‖</mo><msub><mi>𝐩</mi><mrow><mtext>act</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝐩</mi><mrow><mtext>ref</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><msub><mi>ε</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>th</mtext></mrow></msub><mo>]</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{d}(t)=\Bigg(1-\frac{\left\lVert\mathbf{p}_{\text{act},t}-\mathbf{p}_{\text{ref},t}\right\rVert_{2}}{\varepsilon_{d,\text{th}}}\Bigg)\mathbb{I}\!\left[\left\lVert\mathbf{p}_{\text{act},t}-\mathbf{p}_{\text{ref},t}\right\rVert_{2}&lt;\varepsilon_{d,\text{th}}\right],</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(15)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1a.p4" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S2.E16" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E16.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{v}(t)=\max\left(-1,1-\frac{\left\lVert\mathbf{v}_{\text{act},t}\right\rVert_{2}}{\varepsilon_{v,\text{th}}}\right)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>v</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>max</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mfrac><msub><mrow><mo>‖</mo><msub><mi>𝐯</mi><mrow><mtext>act</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><msub><mi>ε</mi><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>th</mtext></mrow></msub></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{v}(t)=\max\left(-1,1-\frac{\left\lVert\mathbf{v}_{\text{act},t}\right\rVert_{2}}{\varepsilon_{v,\text{th}}}\right)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
