<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(16)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1a.p4.1" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS1a.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\varepsilon_{d,\text{th}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ε</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>th</mtext></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varepsilon_{d,\text{th}}</annotation></semantics></math> defines the near-target region (distance threshold), <math id="S2.SS1a.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\varepsilon_{v,\text{th}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ε</mi><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>th</mtext></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varepsilon_{v,\text{th}}</annotation></semantics></math> is the speed threshold, and <math id="S2.SS1a.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{v}_{\text{act},t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐯</mi><mrow><mtext>act</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{v}_{\text{act},t}</annotation></semantics></math> is the planar velocity vector of the active object.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2a" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.2 </span><span id="S2.SS2a.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">World Box</span></h3>

<div id="S2.SS2a.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2a.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Under the batch rendering architecture of Isaac Lab, all environments reside within a unified 3D spatial coordinate system. This proximity often leads to visual interference, as camera sensors may capture features from adjacent environments. To mitigate this visual crosstalk, we encapsulate each environment within a gray cylindrical world box (Fig. <a href="#S2.F8" title="Fig. 8 ‣ B.2 World Box ‣ B Training Details ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>) to effectively isolate per-environment visual information.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F8" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S2.F8.sf1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><img src="2602.18071v1/worldbox_top.png" id="S2.F8.sf1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/268;" width="476" height="268" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F8.sf1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">(a)</span> </span><span id="S2.F8.sf1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Top view</span></figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S2.F8.sf2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><img src="2602.18071v1/worldbox_ego.png" id="S2.F8.sf2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/268;" width="476" height="268" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F8.sf2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">(b)</span> </span><span id="S2.F8.sf2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Ego-View</span></figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F8.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Fig. 8</span>: </span><span id="S2.F8.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">World Boxes for Parallel Training.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.3 </span><span id="S2.SS3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">FOV Design</span></h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We constrain the privileged teacher to use only information recoverable from an egocentric camera by (i) a virtual frustum mask applied to all 3D keypoints and (ii) a center-gated visibility (C-GV) that controls access to the reference target keypoints <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{t}^{ref}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>P</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>f</mi></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{t}^{ref}</annotation></semantics></math>, as shown in Fig. <a href="#S2.F9" title="Fig. 9 ‣ B.3 FOV Design ‣ B Training Details ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F9" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18071v1/2fov.png" id="S2.F9.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:471/265;" width="471" height="265" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F9.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Fig. 9</span>: </span><span id="S2.F9.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Two Primary Mechanisms.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Coordinate conventions.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Let <math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{T}_{wr}=[\mathbf{R}_{wr}|\mathbf{t}_{wr}]\in SE(3)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐓</mi><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐑</mi><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>𝐭</mi><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>E</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{T}_{wr}=[\mathbf{R}_{wr}|\mathbf{t}_{wr}]\in SE(3)</annotation></semantics></math> denote the robot (camera) pose in the world, mapping robot/camera-frame points to world:
<math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{p}_{w}=\mathbf{R}_{wr}\mathbf{p}_{r}+\mathbf{t}_{wr}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐩</mi><mi>w</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐑</mi><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐩</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>𝐭</mi><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{p}_{w}=\mathbf{R}_{wr}\mathbf{p}_{r}+\mathbf{t}_{wr}</annotation></semantics></math>.
We use a camera-aligned robot frame where <math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> points forward, <math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> points left, and <math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math> points up.
Normalized image-plane coordinates <math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(u,v)\in[-1,1]^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(u,v)\in[-1,1]^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> are defined with <math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>u</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u</annotation></semantics></math> right-positive and <math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>v</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v</annotation></semantics></math> down-positive.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">B.3.1 </span>Virtual Egocentric FOV Masking</h4>

<div id="S2.SS3.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Given a world-frame keypoint <math id="S2.SS3.SSS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{p}_{w}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐩</mi><mi>w</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{p}_{w}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}</annotation></semantics></math>, its camera-frame coordinates are</p>
<table id="S2.E17" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E17.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{vis}(\mathbf{p}_{r})=\mathbb{I}\!\left[\begin{array}[]{cr}x&gt;0&amp;\text{and}\\
|y|\leq x\tan(\theta_{h}/2)&amp;\text{and}\\
|z|\leq x\tan(\theta_{v}/2)&amp;\text{and}\\
x\in[d_{\min},d_{\max}]&amp;\end{array}\right]." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>vis</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐩</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mpadded style="width:0.219em;" width="0.219em"><mi>𝕀</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mtable columnspacing="5pt" displaystyle="true" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_right" columnalign="right"><mtext>and</mtext></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>tan</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_right" columnalign="right"><mtext>and</mtext></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>tan</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>v</mi></msub><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_right" columnalign="right"><mtext>and</mtext></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>min</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>max</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mtd><mtd></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{vis}(\mathbf{p}_{r})=\mathbb{I}\!\left[\begin{array}[]{cr}x&gt;0&amp;\text{and}\\
|y|\leq x\tan(\theta_{h}/2)&amp;\text{and}\\
|z|\leq x\tan(\theta_{v}/2)&amp;\text{and}\\
x\in[d_{\min},d_{\max}]&amp;\end{array}\right].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(17)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We use a constant mask value <math id="S2.SS3.SSS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\epsilon}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold-italic" mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\epsilon}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}</annotation></semantics></math> (e.g., <math id="S2.SS3.SSS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\epsilon}=[-10,-10,-10]^{\top}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold-italic" mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\epsilon}=[-10,-10,-10]^{\top}</annotation></semantics></math>).
The masked 3D observation of a keypoint is</p>
<table id="S2.E18" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E18.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\mathbf{p}}_{r}=\begin{cases}\mathbf{p}_{r},&amp;\text{if }\mathrm{vis}(\mathbf{p}_{r})=1\\
\bm{\epsilon},&amp;\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐩</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>r</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mtable columnspacing="5pt" displaystyle="true" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><msub><mi>𝐩</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mtext>if </mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>vis</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐩</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold-italic" mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mi><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mtext>otherwise</mtext><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\mathbf{p}}_{r}=\begin{cases}\mathbf{p}_{r},&amp;\text{if }\mathrm{vis}(\mathbf{p}_{r})=1\\
\bm{\epsilon},&amp;\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(18)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">For C-GV we also compute normalized image-plane coordinates (pinhole, using only FOV):</p>
<table id="S2.E19" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E19.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u=\frac{y}{x\tan(\theta_{h}/2)},\qquad v=\frac{-z}{x\tan(\theta_{v}/2)}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>tan</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>z</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>tan</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>v</mi></msub><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u=\frac{y}{x\tan(\theta_{h}/2)},\qquad v=\frac{-z}{x\tan(\theta_{v}/2)}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(19)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS1.p2.3" class="ltx_p">Note that <math id="S2.SS3.SSS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(u,v)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(u,v)</annotation></semantics></math> is only used for gating; the teacher policy input uses the masked 3D keypoints in equation <a href="#S2.E18" title="In B.3.1 Virtual Egocentric FOV Masking ‣ B.3 FOV Design ‣ B Training Details ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">18</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS3.SSS1.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Fixed-size grouping.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS3.SSS1.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS1.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Each object provides <math id="S2.SS3.SSS1.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> canonical keypoints in its local frame; we transform them to world and then apply equation <a href="#S2.E17" title="In B.3.1 Virtual Egocentric FOV Masking ‣ B.3 FOV Design ‣ B Training Details ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">17</span></a>–equation <a href="#S2.E18" title="In B.3.1 Virtual Egocentric FOV Masking ‣ B.3 FOV Design ‣ B Training Details ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">18</span></a>.
We keep a fixed maximum number of obstacles <math id="S2.SS3.SSS1.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{obs}^{max}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{obs}^{max}</annotation></semantics></math>, sort obstacles by increasing distance to the robot (ties broken by object id), and pad missing obstacles with <math id="S2.SS3.SSS1.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\epsilon}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold-italic" mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\epsilon}</annotation></semantics></math>; extra obstacles are truncated.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">B.3.2 </span>Center-gated Visibility (C-GV) for <math id="S2.SS3.SSS2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{t}^{ref}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>P</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>f</mi></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{t}^{ref}</annotation></semantics></math></h4>

<div id="S2.SS3.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S2.SS3.SSS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{t}^{ref}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>P</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>f</mi></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{t}^{ref}</annotation></semantics></math> is a set of <math id="S2.SS3.SSS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> reference keypoints attached to the <em id="S2.SS3.SSS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">target configuration</em> of the active object relative to the anchor.
At time <math id="S2.SS3.SSS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, we instantiate these reference keypoints in the world by composing the anchor pose with the predefined relative transform for the task category, and then convert them to the camera frame and mask them using equation <a href="#S2.E18" title="In B.3.1 Virtual Egocentric FOV Masking ‣ B.3 FOV Design ‣ B Training Details ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">18</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To prevent exploiting <math id="S2.SS3.SSS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{t}^{ref}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>P</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>f</mi></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{t}^{ref}</annotation></semantics></math> while ignoring the anchor, we reveal <math id="S2.SS3.SSS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{t}^{ref}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>P</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>f</mi></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{t}^{ref}</annotation></semantics></math> <em id="S2.SS3.SSS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">only if</em> the anchor lies (i) within the virtual FOV and (ii) inside a central gate in the image plane.
Let <math id="S2.SS3.SSS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{c}_{anc,w}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐜</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{c}_{anc,w}</annotation></semantics></math> be the anchor centroid in world (we use the object’s pose center; if unavailable, the mean of its <math id="S2.SS3.SSS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> keypoints).
Compute <math id="S2.SS3.SSS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{c}_{anc,r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐜</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{c}_{anc,r}</annotation></semantics></math> and its <math id="S2.SS3.SSS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(u_{anc},v_{anc})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(u_{anc},v_{anc})</annotation></semantics></math> using equation <a href="#S2.E19" title="In B.3.1 Virtual Egocentric FOV Masking ‣ B.3 FOV Design ‣ B Training Details ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">19</span></a>.
Define</p>

</table>
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS3.SSS2.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(u_{gate},v_{gate})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(u_{gate},v_{gate})</annotation></semantics></math> specifies the central gated region.
Finally, the teacher’s observable reference keypoints are</p>

</table>
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS2.p2.3" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS3.SSS2.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}_{3d}(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}_{3d}(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> applies equation <a href="#S2.E18" title="In B.3.1 Virtual Egocentric FOV Masking ‣ B.3 FOV Design ‣ B Training Details ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">18</span></a> element-wise to the <math id="S2.SS3.SSS2.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> reference keypoints.
Under these constraints, the teacher observes grouped masked keypoints
<math id="S2.SS3.SSS2.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\tilde{P}_{t}^{act},\tilde{P}_{t}^{anc},\tilde{P}_{t}^{obs},\tilde{P}_{t}^{ref}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>P</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>P</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>P</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>P</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>f</mi></mrow></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\tilde{P}_{t}^{act},\tilde{P}_{t}^{anc},\tilde{P}_{t}^{obs},\tilde{P}_{t}^{ref}\}</annotation></semantics></math> and the previous action <math id="S2.SS3.SSS2.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{t-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{t-1}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.4 </span><span id="S2.SS4.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Front Pusher on Robot</span></h3>

<div id="S2.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To address the sensing dead zone (approx. 15 cm) of the depth camera, a pusher is integrated into the robot base as shown in Fig. <a href="#S2.F10" title="Fig. 10 ‣ B.4 Front Pusher on Robot ‣ B Training Details ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>. This end-effector features a 7.5 cm protrusion and a 14 cm <math id="S2.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> 10 cm frontal profile. This design ensures that objects remain within the reliable depth-sensing manifold during interaction, while maintaining a form factor consistent with the robot’s width.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F10" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18071v1/pusher.png" id="S2.F10.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:333/250;" width="333" height="250" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F10.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Fig. 10</span>: </span><span id="S2.F10.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Robot with Pusher and its Collider.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S2.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">While the 7.5 cm protrusion effectively mitigates the depth camera’s sensing dead zone, it introduces a significant longitudinal offset between the contact interface and the robot’s Instantaneous Center of Rotation (ICR). This extension of the moment arm (lever arm) dictates that any off-center contact force results in a disproportionately large parasitic yaw moment. Consequently, even minor misalignments in the pushing vector are amplified into substantial rotational disturbances, complicating the maintenance of a stable heading during rectilinear manipulation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Despite the inherent dynamical instabilities introduced by the extended pusher, our learning-based agent demonstrates remarkable performance and adaptability. This success underscores the robustness of the reinforcement learning framework in internalizing and compensating for complex, non-linear contact dynamics. The policy effectively learns to modulate its control signals to suppress the parasitic yaw moments, achieving precise manipulation even within a constrained dynamical manifold.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Interestingly, an emergent behavior was observed during our ablation study on Restricted Observations for the RL Teacher. When the teacher is granted unconstrained global perception (rendering the depth camera’s sensing dead zone irrelevant), it consistently converges to an unconventional strategy: pushing the object with the robot’s rear chassis—the side without the pusher integrated.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS4.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Guided by temporally decayed completion rewards, the global teacher prioritizes execution efficiency and stability. By utilizing the rear side, the agent effectively minimizes the moment arm between the contact point and the robot’s center of rotation. This strategy reduces the sensitivity to alignment errors and eliminates the aforementioned ’snaking’ effect, allowing for faster and more stable task completion. This phenomenon further validates that the pusher serves as a perceptual scaffold that, while essential for egocentric sensing, imposes a dynamical penalty that the agent must learn to navigate.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3a" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">C </span><span id="S3a.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Real World Robot System Setup</span></h2>

<div id="S3a.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3a.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We used a TurtleBot3 Burger as the mobile robot platform. The robot uses two servo motors and one passive ball caster. The two actuators provide a maximal translation velocity of <math id="S3a.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.22\text{ m/s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.22</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext> m/s</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.22\text{ m/s}</annotation></semantics></math> and a maximal rotation velocity of <math id="S3a.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2.84\text{ rad/s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2.84</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext> rad/s</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2.84\text{ rad/s}</annotation></semantics></math>. A 3D-printed pusher was mounted in front of the robot. The heading of the robot is reconfigured to the opposite of the default direction, such that the ball caster is in the front and the two drive motors are in the rear, allowing a longer lever arm for the actuator. Real-world pushers are equipped with bumper strips on both sides, as shown in Fig. <a href="#S3.F11" title="Fig. 11 ‣ C Real World Robot System Setup ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a>, to ensure alignment between the real-world pusher and the pusher’s collider box in the simulation, avoid exploiting gaps along the pusher’s sides to manipulate the boxes.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3a.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3a.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The robot is equipped with an NVIDIA Jetson Nano, running Ubuntu 20.04 with ROS1 for camera and low-level action control. An Intel RealSense D435i camera is connected to Jetson, mounted on the top of the robot to provide RGB-D egocentric view. The RGB sensor of the camera is set to <math id="S3a.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="20\text{cm}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>20</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>cm</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">20\text{cm}</annotation></semantics></math> above and <math id="S3a.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5\text{cm}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>cm</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5\text{cm}</annotation></semantics></math> behind the ball caster, pitching down <math id="S3a.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="11.5^{\circ}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>11.5</mn><mo>∘</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">11.5^{\circ}</annotation></semantics></math> from the horizon.We used a python wrapper of librealsense2 to handle RealSense Camera utilities. The RGB image is captured at a resolution of <math id="S3a.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="320\times 240" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>320</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>240</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">320\times 240</annotation></semantics></math>. The depth image is captured at a resolution of <math id="S3a.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="480\times 270" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>480</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>270</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">480\times 270</annotation></semantics></math>, and aligned with the RGB image before down-sampling together to a resolution of <math id="S3a.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="240\times 180" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>240</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>180</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">240\times 180</annotation></semantics></math>. The camera initially operates at a base frequency of 30Hz, with varying delays depending on the image processing method employed.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F11" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18071v1/pusher_design.png" id="S3.F11.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:333/260;" width="333" height="260" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F11.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Fig. 11</span>: </span><span id="S3.F11.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Pusher of the real robot.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3a.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3a.p3.1" class="ltx_p">A laptop equipped with an Intel Ultra 9 275HX CPU and an NVIDIA RTX 5080 GPU runs Ubuntu 22.04 and serves as the server for computation. The communication between the robot and the server is established via WebSocket. Specifically, the robot continuously streams the egocentric RGB-D observations to the server over Wi-Fi. On the server side, the received image are decoded and undergo post-processing and segmentation. The resulting processed image patches are used as inputs to the control policy. The policy then performs real-time inference to generate velocity commands, which are transmitted back to the robot at <math id="S3a.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>25Hz. The robot executes the received velocity commands through its local ROS1 control stack.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4a" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">D </span><span id="S4a.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Image Processing</span></h2>

<section id="S4.SS1a" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.1 </span><span id="S4.SS1a.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">RGB Image</span></h3>

<div id="S4.SS1a.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1a.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The experiments were conducted in a <math id="S4.SS1a.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3\text{m}\times 3\text{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>m</mtext></mrow><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>m</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3\text{m}\times 3\text{m}</annotation></semantics></math> gray arena containing five boxes of distinct colors: red, green, blue, violet, and brown. Upon receiving the egocentric RGB stream from the robot, the server performs color-based segmentation using HSV thresholding. This process isolates the boxes from the gray background, generating binary masks that are subsequently used to filter the depth images. The specific HSV threshold ranges adopted for each color are detailed in Table <a href="#S4.T6" title="TABLE VI ‣ D.1 RGB Image ‣ D Image Processing ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">VI</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T6" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S4.T6.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">TABLE VI</span>: </span><span id="S4.T6.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
HSV threshold ranges used for box segmentation in real-world experiments with OpenCV convention. Here, hue is represented on a circular scale with <math id="S4.T6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H\in[0,179]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0,179</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H\in[0,179]</annotation></semantics></math> (hence the red mask wraps around the boundary and is implemented as <math id="S4.T6.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H\in[179,179]\cup[0,7]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>179,179</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>∪</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H\in[179,179]\cup[0,7]</annotation></semantics></math>). Saturation and value use <math id="S4.T6.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S\in[0,255]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0,255</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S\in[0,255]</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.T6.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V\in[0,255]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0,255</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V\in[0,255]</annotation></semantics></math>.
</span></figcaption>

<td id="S4.T6.5.1.5.9" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding-left:7.0pt;padding-right:7.0pt;"><span id="S4.T6.5.1.5.9.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">255</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S4.T6.5.1.6" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S4.T6.5.1.6.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row" style="padding-left:7.0pt;padding-right:7.0pt;"><span id="S4.T6.5.1.6.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">Violet</span></th>
<td id="S4.T6.5.1.6.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding-left:7.0pt;padding-right:7.0pt;"><span id="S4.T6.5.1.6.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">150</span></td>
<td id="S4.T6.5.1.6.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding-left:7.0pt;padding-right:7.0pt;"><span id="S4.T6.5.1.6.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">180</span></td>
<td id="S4.T6.5.1.6.4" class="ltx_td" style="padding-left:7.0pt;padding-right:7.0pt;"></td>

</table>
</span></div>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2a" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.2 </span><span id="S4.SS2a.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Depth Image</span></h3>

<div id="S4.SS2a.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2a.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To reduce background clutter and sensor noise irrelevant to the target object, we apply the binary foreground masks obtained from the RGB image to the depth images. In the real-world experiments, the raw depth output from the Intel RealSense D435i suffers from significant noise across the sensing range, and depth measurements for the top surfaces of the boxes are frequently subject to dropouts. To mitigate these issues, we investigated four depth postprocessing strategies. Comparison videos of the different depth processing methods are available on our website: <a href="https://ai4ce.github.io/EgoPush/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://ai4ce.github.io/EgoPush/</a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2a.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2a.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2a.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(A) Learning-based denoising.</span> We evaluated the state-of-the-art Camera Depth Model (CDM) for RealSense D435i from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite>. This model fuses RGB and depth modalities to guide depth denoising. While CDM yields fine-grained reconstruction and effectively preserves top-surface details, it incurs a prohibitive inference latency (<math id="S4.SS2a.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>50ms per frame) despite server-side deployment, rendering it unsuitable for our real-time control pipeline.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2a.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2a.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2a.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(B) Onboard postprocessing.</span> We followed the depth filtering stack in  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">50</a>]</cite>, applying hole-filling, spatial, and temporal filters sequentially to the depth image on Jetson Nano. However, this approach yields suboptimal results that the top surfaces exhibit strong temporal flickering at close range and often disappear entirely at longer distances. Furthermore, the processing latency on the robot’s onboard hardware is relatively high (<math id="S4.SS2a.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>15ms per frame).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2a.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2a.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2a.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(C) Median-depth filling(ours).</span> As a baseline, we implemented a constant-fill method that replaces all pixels within the masked region with the median depth value. This approach produces highly stable depth maps and facilitates sim-to-real alignment, performing well in our setup with simple geometric objects. The method is deployed on the server with negligible latency (<math id="S4.SS2a.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>2ms per frame). However, because it discards all intra-object geometric details, its ability to generalize to objects with more complex geometric structures is inherently limited.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2a.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2a.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2a.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(D) Navier–Stokes inpainting(ours).</span> Our final implemented solution employs Navier–Stokes inpainting <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite> within the masked region, and during simulation training we inject random noise into the depth input to better approximate real-world sensing conditions. Although it recovers less geometric detail than the learning-based CDM, it provides greater stability compared to onboard postprocessing and improved generalization relative to median-depth filling. Empirically, this method achieves a task success rate comparable to the median-filling baseline while retaining significantly more geometric information. It is deployed on the server side with a computational cost similar to the median-fill method (<math id="S4.SS2a.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>2ms per frame).</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5a" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">E </span><span id="S5a.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Additional Experiment Results</span></h2>

<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">E.1 </span><span id="S5.SS1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Different Boxes shapes</span></h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We further evaluate the <em id="S5.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">student</em> policy on different kinds of object geometries to probe its generalization beyond the training cuboid. Specifically, we replace the active object with a cylinder or a triangular prism, while keeping the sensing setup, action bounds, termination conditions, and evaluation protocol unchanged.
As reported in Table <a href="#S5.T7" title="TABLE VII ‣ E.1 Different Boxes shapes ‣ E Additional Experiment Results ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">VII</span></a>, the student maintains a near-perfect ReachBox rate for both geometries, indicating that the perception-and-approach sub-skill transfers well across shapes.
However, the overall SR drops to <math id="S5.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="67.48\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>67.48</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">67.48\%</annotation></semantics></math> on the cylinder and <math id="S5.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="54.30\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>54.30</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">54.30\%</annotation></semantics></math> on the prism, with noticeably longer ExecTime and TrajLen for the prism. The gap between ReachBox and SR suggests that most failures occur in the interaction phase to maintain stable contact and completing the final alignment, where geometry-dependent contact dynamics can amplify small control errors over long horizons.
Figure <a href="#S5.F12" title="Fig. 12 ‣ E.1 Different Boxes shapes ‣ E Additional Experiment Results ‣ EgoPush: Learning End-to-End Egocentric Multi-Object Rearrangement for Mobile Robots" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a> provides representative qualitative rollouts for the two geometries.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T7" class="ltx_table">

</figure>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">E.2 </span><span id="S5.SS2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Ours accuracy</span></h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For the cuboid pushing task, the proposed student model is evaluated using a
<em id="S5.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">nearest-distance–based accuracy metric</em>. Since the student policy does
not have access to the target tag during execution, performance is assessed by
measuring the Euclidean distance between the final box position and its
corresponding (invisible) target tag in the workspace.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To normalize the error magnitude, the distance is bounded by the
training-time distance threshold, which serves as the maximum admissible error.
The normalized error is computed as the ratio between the nearest geometric
distance and this threshold. Under this evaluation protocol, the student model
achieves an average error rate of approximately <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="13.3\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>13.3</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">13.3\%</annotation></semantics></math> on the cuboid pushing
task.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Let <math id="S5.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{p}_{\text{box}}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐩</mi><mtext>box</mtext></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{p}_{\text{box}}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the final planar position
of the pushed box, and <math id="S5.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{p}_{\text{tag}}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐩</mi><mtext>tag</mtext></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{p}_{\text{tag}}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the
position of the corresponding target tag. The nearest-distance error is defined
as</p>
<table id="S5.E22" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S5.E22.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d=\left\|\mathbf{p}_{\text{box}}-\mathbf{p}_{\text{tag}}\right\|_{2}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐩</mi><mtext>box</mtext></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝐩</mi><mtext>tag</mtext></msub></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d=\left\|\mathbf{p}_{\text{box}}-\mathbf{p}_{\text{tag}}\right\|_{2}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(22)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Given the training-time distance threshold <math id="S5.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\varepsilon_{\text{train}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ε</mi><mtext>train</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varepsilon_{\text{train}}</annotation></semantics></math>, the
normalized accuracy score is computed as</p>
<table id="S5.E23" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S5.E23.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{Acc}=1-\frac{\min\!\left(d,\,\varepsilon_{\text{train}}\right)}{\varepsilon_{\text{train}}}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>Acc</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mpadded style="width:1.653em;" width="1.653em"><mi>min</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>ε</mi><mtext>train</mtext></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><msub><mi>ε</mi><mtext>train</mtext></msub></mfrac></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{Acc}=1-\frac{\min\!\left(d,\,\varepsilon_{\text{train}}\right)}{\varepsilon_{\text{train}}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(23)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Accordingly, the corresponding error rate is defined as</p>
<table id="S5.E24" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S5.E24.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{Error}=\frac{\min\!\left(d,\,\varepsilon_{\text{train}}\right)}{\varepsilon_{\text{train}}}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>Error</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mpadded style="width:1.653em;" width="1.653em"><mi>min</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>ε</mi><mtext>train</mtext></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><msub><mi>ε</mi><mtext>train</mtext></msub></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{Error}=\frac{\min\!\left(d,\,\varepsilon_{\text{train}}\right)}{\varepsilon_{\text{train}}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(24)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</article>

      all.</p>
